title: Arise and eat (1 Kings 19:1–8)
hook: exhausted Elijah wants to die; an angel brings food and says "Arise and eat"

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Mount Carmel, Elijah asked a silent crowd how long they would halt between two opinions. Did you settle one thing you'd been hovering over? Today, soon after the fire, the same prophet is running for his life. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A message arrives from the palace. Queen Jezebel has heard what happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a promise: by this time tomorrow, you'll be dead. The man who stood alone against a mountain full of prophets doesn't stand this time. He runs. South, out of the kingdom, to Beer-sheba. He leaves his servant there and keeps going, alone, a day's journey into the wilderness. Then he sits down under a broom tree, a scrubby desert bush. And the prophet who faced down a whole mountain says he's done.
screen: `A THREAT FROM THE QUEEN.` → `A DAY INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `UNDER A BROOM TREE.`

segments.voice: His words are blunt. It is enough. Now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am not better than my fathers. Then he lies down and falls asleep. Notice the timing. This isn't Elijah after a failure. It's Elijah right after Carmel. Fire fell from heaven at his word, and now he's under a bush asking to die. The text doesn't scold him for it. It doesn't call him weak or faithless. It just tells us what came next. An angel touches him and says: "Arise and eat." He looks, and there by his head is a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He eats, he drinks, and he lies back down. That's it. No lecture. No explanation of the big picture. Then the angel comes a second time, touches him again, and says it again: arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you. He gets up, eats, drinks, and in the strength of that food, the text says, he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. Look at the order. Before anyone talks to Elijah about his calling, his fear, or his future, someone feeds him and lets him sleep. Twice. The help comes as bread and water and rest. Some readers notice how tender this scene is: the God who sent fire on Carmel sends a meal under a bush. The great conversation is still coming, on the mountain. But first, the body. A tired person can't hear much of anything. So the first word from heaven is the plainest one possible. Get up. Eat something.
screen: `IT IS ENOUGH.` · `A CAKE AND A JAR OF WATER.` · then, large: `ARISE AND EAT.` · then: `THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat and rest when overwhelmed. Settle where you are. Ask your body a plain question: when did I last eat, drink water, or rest? Don't argue with the answer. Let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen. Take a slow breath in and a longer breath out. If something heavy is pressing on you today, set it beside you for these two minutes, the way Elijah's journey waited while he slept. The decisions can wait for a fed and rested you. When the bell ends, if you can, get a glass of water or something small to eat. The bell holds the time.
Broom tree. Where an exhausted Elijah collapsed and asked to die, before an angel told him to eat. Today's word.
Your line: but first, the body. Today, when everything feels like too much, start with the simple things first: water, food, a few minutes of rest. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's flight to the wilderness as part of the book of Kings, and it is read in synagogue as a haftarah; the scene is often remembered as a picture of care for someone at the end of their strength.

myth: Elijah fled right after losing on Carmel
he fled right after the fire fell, soon after his victory.
the angel woke him twice to eat
the second time adding: the journey is too great for thee.
the angel rebuked Elijah for despairing
the text has no rebuke here, only food, water and rest.

fork.setup: you're the angel. the prophet who brought fire down is lying under a bush, asking to die. what do you do first?
options: remind him of his victory on Carmel.
wake him and give him food and water.
fork.reveal: the angel says arise and eat, lets him sleep again, and feeds him a second time. the talk comes later.

original.note: Hebrew: arise, eat, the angel's words in 1 Kings 19:5 and 19:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle meal.
what it means: before anyone talks to the worn-out prophet, he is fed and allowed to sleep.
what a scholar hears: forty days and nights to Horeb, where Moses too stayed forty days and nights (Deuteronomy 9:9).
